open-question.question: What function-derived subject does the bootstrap commit carry, given it has no milestone id to serve as descriptor (a marker such as Workflow-bootstrap: with what descriptor), and is the commit subject-only like the other setup skills or does it carry a body naming which files were created versus preserved?
open-question.recommendation: A constant, searchable subject-only `Workflow-bootstrap: milestones` names the thing the commit acts on, matching the other setup markers, while a body naming created-versus-preserved items only repeats what the path-scoped commit's diff already records and a plugin-named descriptor would name the mechanism rather than the object.
open-question.alternative: The commit carries the constant subject `Workflow-bootstrap: milestones` and no body. The descriptor names the scaffold root that the bootstrap creates, since there is no milestone id to use. This matches the subject-only `Milestone-definition:`, `Milestone-activation:` and `Milestone-finish:` setup commits. The subject is fixed and searchable with `git log --grep='^Workflow-bootstrap: '`. It follows the house `<Marker>: <descriptor>` shape that the commit procedure's SUBJECT input and design claim 12's zero-unknown-subjects metric expect, and it adds no body logic. Nothing is lost by leaving out a body: the path-scoped commit's own diff already shows whether `milestones/README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` were created or appended to. The descriptor says almost nothing that the marker doesn't already say. If a later re-run repairs a partial scaffold (for example a README that has lost its `Current milestone:` line, which step 2 does not count as initialized), it makes a second commit with the same subject. The two commits can then only be told apart by their diffs.

The commit carries the constant subject `Workflow-bootstrap: cairn` and no body. The descriptor names the workflow being installed rather than a path. In a consuming project's history, where the other subjects belong to that project, the subject says which tool put `milestones/` and the `## Milestone Workflow` section of `CLAUDE.md` there. It keeps the fixed, searchable, subject-only form. The runtime files already name the plugin in their `cairn:<agent>` dispatch names, so no new naming rule is needed. The descriptor names the plugin, not the thing the commit acts on. That breaks the pattern of every other descriptor, which names the milestone, question or task that the commit touched. The plugin name also becomes a literal in the committed history of every bootstrapped project, so a rename would leave old histories using the old name.

The descriptor lists exactly the paths the pass committed, taken from the same PATHS set the skill passes to the commit procedure: `Workflow-bootstrap: milestones/README.md, CLAUDE.md`, or just `milestones/README.md` when `CLAUDE.md` was left alone. The commit has no body. The subject shows what the bootstrap wrote without opening the commit. It is built from values the skill already has at edit time (step 5 knows whether it touched `CLAUDE.md`), with no content inspection, and it stays subject-only. Unlike every other marker, the subject changes from run to run and has no stable descriptor to search on. It repeats the file list that the commit's diff already records. It also makes the descriptor slot hold a list, which the existing `<Marker>: <descriptor>` subjects never do.

The commit carries a constant subject such as `Workflow-bootstrap: milestones`. Its BODY has one line per scaffold item, recording whether that item was created, had a section inserted, or was preserved untouched (`milestones/`, `milestones/README.md`, the `## Milestone Workflow` section of `CLAUDE.md`). This keeps step 6's created-versus-preserved itemization in the commit. History keeps the one fact the diff cannot show: which items already existed and were deliberately left alone. That matters most if the console report shrinks to a single status line. It uses the commit procedure's existing optional BODY input, as `Principle-capture:` and the recommendation commits already do. It is the only setup commit with a body, and most of that body repeats what the diff shows. Preserved files are not in PATHS at all, so the body describes files the commit does not contain. Whether the body adds anything depends on how the reporting-shape question is settled: it only preserves information when the console itemization is removed.

open-question.question: Does the git work-tree check run before or after the Python check, does a project failing both get one combined stop message or two separate stops on successive runs, and does the git check run on every invocation including a re-run on an already-bootstrapped project, as the Python check does?

depends-on.question: Git-check remedy wording
depends-on.option: Four-part stop, user runs git init

open-question.recommendation: Both checks run on every invocation as separate stops with their own four-part message, so the health-check property is kept and step 1's template is reused rather than restructured, and the git check goes first because it guards the more basic capability every committing skill needs and is the failure a fresh directory most often hits, with the cheapest remedy; the opening-paragraph and skill-reference edits it forces are already in the milestone's docs work.
open-question.alternative: Put the git work-tree check first, ahead of the Python check, with both still running on every invocation before state detection. Each check stops on its own with its own message, so a project that fails both learns about git first and about Python on the next run. The failure most likely in a fresh directory is reported first, and it has the cheapest remedy (git init). Commit capability is also the more basic requirement, because every committing skill needs it while only the question skills need python3. Each stop still keeps its own single four-part message. Step 1 is renumbered and the Python check is no longer the opening check the skill's opening paragraph describes, so the prose and docs/skill-reference.md that present the Python check as the first thing the skill does need edits. A project failing both still needs two runs.

Keep step 1 as it is and add the git work-tree check as a new step right after it, before state detection. Both checks run on every invocation. Each check stops on its own with its own message, so a project that fails both is stopped by the Python check first and hears about git only on the next run. It extends the existing step 1 template without changing it. Each stop keeps its single four-part message unchanged, the Python check's wording and position stay as they are, and a re-run on an already-bootstrapped project gets both checks the same way. A project missing both prerequisites needs two failed runs before it learns everything it must fix. The order puts the rarer failure (no suitable python3) ahead of the one a fresh empty directory is most likely to hit (not a git repository).

Run both checks on every invocation before state detection, always evaluating both, and stop once with a single message when either fails. The message covers each failing prerequisite in the four-part shape (what it looked for, what it found, the remedy) and ends with one closing line saying that a re-run completes the bootstrap. A project failing both prerequisites learns everything it must fix in one run. The order question goes away except as the order of sections in the message, which matters most for first-time users bootstrapping an empty directory. Step 1's one-check, one-message template has to be restructured into a collect-then-report step, so the Python check's stop logic and message are rewritten rather than left alone. The stop message is longer and has more branches, and how it is laid out depends on how the sibling question about git-check remedy wording settles the git message's shape.

Keep the Python check first and on every invocation. Run the git work-tree check after state detection and only on the path that will write, so a re-run on an already-bootstrapped project stops as "already initialized" without checking for git. The check is required only where it matters. A no-op re-run writes nothing and commits nothing, so it has no need for a git repository, and the scaffolding step's precondition stays next to the commit it protects. It departs from the Python check's every-invocation rule, so the two prerequisites behave differently. A re-run would no longer serve as a health check: an already-bootstrapped project that is not a git repository gets told it is initialized, and then every later committing skill fails at the commit procedure, which assumes a work tree and checks for none.

open-question.question: When the project is not a git repository, does the stop message tell the user to run git init and re-run, or does the skill offer to initialize the repository itself, and does the message follow the four-part shape of the Python stop message (what it looked for, what it found, the remedy, that a re-run completes the bootstrap)?

recommendation.option: Four-part stop, user runs git init

open-question.recommendation: It matches the goal's "stopping before it writes anything", copies the stop shape the Python check already has so both prerequisites read alike, never prompts so it behaves identically in a headless chain, and keeps a repository-creating decision with the user; offering to run git init adds a prompt no chain can answer and creates a .git outside the skill's own paths, and a terse one-liner gives a wrong remedy when git itself is missing.

alternative.id: Four-part stop, user runs git init

open-question.alternative: The git check copies the step 1 Python template. It stops before any write and prints one message giving what it looked for (a git work tree at the workspace root), what it found (either the `git` executable is missing or the directory is not a work tree), the remedy that fits (install git, or run `git init` in the workspace root), and that running `/init-milestone-base-workflow` again completes the bootstrap with nothing to undo. The skill never runs `git init` itself. It matches the goal's wording "stopping before it writes anything when the project is not a git repository" and reuses a stop shape the skill already has, so the two prerequisite checks read the same. It also never prompts, so it behaves the same in a headless chain. Choosing where the repository lives stays with the user, which matters when the workspace root might be the wrong directory for it. The most common case, a fresh project with no repository yet, always costs a stop, a manual `git init`, and a second run. If the "Work-tree check strictness" question settles on stricter pass rules, the "what it found" part needs more cases, such as being inside a larger repository but not at its top level.

When no work tree is found, the skill asks the user whether to run `git init` in the workspace root. If the user agrees, it initializes the repository and continues the bootstrap in the same run. If the user declines, or no one can answer, it falls back to a four-part stop message like the Python one. Interactive users get through the common fresh-project case in one run without leaving the skill, and nothing is created without explicit consent. It adds a consent prompt that no other prerequisite check has, and that prompt cannot be answered in a headless chain. It also stretches the goal's "stopping before it writes anything": with consent, the skill creates a `.git` directory, which is outside the paths it owns. The skill would also have to handle a brand-new repository with no commits and no configured identity before its first commit could succeed.

The skill stops before any write with a single short line, for example "not a git repository — run git init and re-run /init-milestone-base-workflow". It does not follow the four-part shape and does not tell a missing `git` executable apart from a directory that is not a repository. It is the smallest runtime change. It also fits the terse console-reporting style the other committing skills use. The skill's two prerequisite checks would report failures in different shapes. When git itself is not installed, the one-line remedy is wrong, and nothing in the message says so. The user loses the found-versus-expected detail that the Python check deliberately gives.

open-question.question: When CLAUDE.md or milestones/README.md already carries uncommitted changes before the bootstrap runs (for example a CLAUDE.md just written by /init and never committed), does the bootstrap's path-scoped commit sweep those unrelated hunks into its own commit, stop before writing, or proceed and note it?
open-question.recommendation: The bootstrap hands its own paths to the shared commit procedure exactly as finish-current-milestone already does with CLAUDE.md, adding no probe, stop, prompt, or advisory: a stop or confirmation blocks the very /init-first flow the question names and fails in a headless chain, hunk-level staging breaks the procedure's no-content-inspection contract, and the swept hunks are visible in the commit diff while in the common case they are the CLAUDE.md the user just wrote and wants committed, so an advisory would only nag on the expected flow.
open-question.alternative: Keep the commit as it is. After the bootstrap writes, it hands its own paths (milestones/README.md, and CLAUDE.md when step 5 edited it) to the shared commit procedure unchanged, so any hunks that were already uncommitted in those files go into the bootstrap's commit. It does not check for them first and does not mention them. The bootstrap ends up doing exactly what finish-current-milestone step 8 already does with CLAUDE.md, so there is no new mechanism, no new stop, no new report line and nothing to prompt for. A headless run always ends with a clean tree. In the common case the question names (a CLAUDE.md just written by /init, untracked, which the bootstrap then appends to), committing that file whole is probably what the user wanted anyway. The commit carries content the bootstrap did not write, under a subject that credits all of it to the bootstrap. A user's half-finished edits to either file get committed without their knowledge or consent, and nothing in the report or the commit tells them that happened.

Add a check before any write, placed alongside the Python and git prerequisite checks. It runs `git status --porcelain` scoped to the paths the bootstrap is about to write, which step 2 already knows. If any of them is dirty or untracked, the bootstrap stops without writing and prints a message naming the path, telling the user to commit or stash it and saying that a re-run completes the bootstrap. The bootstrap's commit only ever holds its own changes, so its subject stays accurate and the user's work is never committed for them. The stop writes nothing, so a re-run has nothing to undo. This is the same stop shape as the existing prerequisite check. It blocks the exact case the question names. An untracked CLAUDE.md fresh from /init counts as dirty, so anyone who runs /init first has to make their own commit before the bootstrap will run. In a headless chain that shows up as a failed step rather than a finished one. It also adds a third stop path and message to a skill whose goal is to add just one new prerequisite. Where the check sits relative to the other prerequisite checks and state detection depends on how the prerequisite-ordering question settles.

Before writing, record which of its own paths were already dirty. Commit them together with the bootstrap's own changes as the shared commit procedure does now. Then, next to the one fixed status line, print an advisory naming each path whose earlier uncommitted changes went into the commit. Nothing blocks, so both the /init-first flow and a headless chain finish with a clean tree, and the user is told that unrelated hunks went into the commit, which git history alone would never show. The advisory fits the existing reporting rule: git itself does not record that those hunks were already there, so it is a decision-critical advisory of the kind that rule allows. The commit still carries content credited to the wrong source. The user finds out only after their edits are committed, and undoing that means amending or reverting by hand. It also adds a pre-write status probe and a conditional advisory to a report the reporting-shape question is trying to reduce to one terse line.

Use the dirty-store guard from capture-milestone-principle-updates as the pattern. If either path the bootstrap is about to write is already dirty or untracked, it prints a one-line notice and asks once whether to proceed. On yes, the pending edits become the base the bootstrap writes over, and the whole file is committed. On no, it stops without writing. The user explicitly agrees before any of their own edits are committed, and the mechanism already exists in the codebase, so it is not a new idea. The /init-first case costs a single keypress instead of a manual commit. A confirmation prompt conflicts with the milestone's headless goal. A `-p` run has nobody to answer it, so the bootstrap either fails or has to pick a default that turns into one of the other options in that situation. It also makes the bootstrap the second skill that stops to ask a question at the start of a run.

Stage only the bootstrap's own change: the appended Milestone Workflow section, or the Current milestone section inserted into milestones/README.md. Build the staged version from the HEAD blob plus that change, and leave the user's earlier hunks in the working tree, uncommitted and still theirs. The commit subject is exactly accurate and the user's work is never committed or blocked. It is the only option that fully separates the two sets of changes. It needs content-aware, hunk-level staging, which the shared commit procedure rules out: it stages named paths whole and never inspects content. The mechanism would exist in this one skill only. It has no sensible result for the /init case, where CLAUDE.md is untracked and has no HEAD version, so the commit would record a CLAUDE.md containing nothing but the workflow section. And the tree stays dirty afterwards, which is what the milestone set out to end.

open-question.question: Does the bootstrap's step 6 report become the one fixed identifier-free status line the other committing skills print, with a distinct line for the already-initialized no-op path, and does the suggestion to run /init and /define-milestone-goal next survive as an advisory or get cut along with the created-versus-preserved itemization?
open-question.recommendation: Once the bootstrap commits, the terse-reporting invariant applies to it without exception: one fixed line such as "Workflow bootstrapped." plus a distinct already-initialized no-op line, because the commit diff already shows which files were created or appended, a newly created CLAUDE.md holding only the workflow section is likewise visible in that diff so the /init advisory is not a git-absent signal, and next-step pointers are exactly the handoff output the other setup skills deliberately omit.
open-question.alternative: Step 6 becomes one fixed terse status line such as `Workflow bootstrapped.`, and the already-initialized stop in step 2 prints one different no-op line. The created-versus-preserved list, the pointer-initialized line, the numbered next steps and the step-5 suggestion to run /init are all removed, matching finish-current-milestone, which prints no next-step or handoff pointer. It follows the CLAUDE.md terse-reporting invariant with no exception. The skill then reports the same way as define-milestone-goal, goto-next-milestone, specify-milestone-starting-state and finish-current-milestone. Once the bootstrap commits, the commit diff already shows which files were created or edited, so the itemized list only repeats git. A first-time user gets no pointer to /init. specify-milestone-starting-state, derive-tasks and the completion procedure all read the project's environment context from CLAUDE.md, and the commit diff does not show that this context is missing. The user also gets no hint that /define-milestone-goal comes next, even though the bootstrap is usually the first Cairn skill they run.

Step 6 prints one fixed terse status line and step 2's already-initialized stop prints one different no-op line. The /init suggestion stays as a single fixed advisory printed only on runs where step 5 created CLAUDE.md. The itemization, the pointer line and the /define-milestone-goal next step are removed. It keeps the one piece of output that fits the invariant's exception for git-absent, decision-critical advisories. A newly created CLAUDE.md that holds only the workflow section leaves later skills without environment context, and neither git nor any other skill says so. Step 5 already knows at edit time whether it created the file, so the condition is easy to check. The bootstrap becomes the only setup skill that prints a next-step advisory, so the rule "no handoff pointers" gets its first exception. The trigger is also imperfect. A user who ran /init earlier but never committed it, or whose existing CLAUDE.md has no real project documentation, gets no advisory. Showing it every time CLAUDE.md is created may also nag a user who plans to write CLAUDE.md by hand.

Step 6 prints one fixed terse status line followed by one fixed next-steps line naming /init and then /define-milestone-goal on every successful run. Step 2's already-initialized stop prints one different no-op line. Only the created-versus-preserved list and the pointer line are removed. The onboarding help stays complete and predictable. The skill runs once per project, usually for someone new to the workflow, and a short fixed pointer to the next two skills is the least surprising way to finish that first run. The output also stays free of identifiers and does not vary from run to run. This makes the bootstrap a clear onboarding exception to "no next-step or handoff pointer", which is exactly the kind of rule a later editor might tidy away. It also tells users to run /init even when CLAUDE.md is already fully documented. A headless chain that goes straight to /define-milestone-goal ignores the text anyway.

Step 6 keeps its current multi-line report: what was created versus preserved, the pointer initialized to none, and the numbered next steps. At most it adds that the files were committed. The already-initialized stop keeps its current free-form "already initialized" report. It changes the least. The goal of this milestone is about committing and the git prerequisite, not about reporting, so this avoids widening scope. The one-time setup skill also keeps its most informative and friendliest output. Once the bootstrap commits, it becomes the only committing skill that still prints a multi-line, per-item success report. That goes against the CLAUDE.md invariant that success output is one fixed, identifier-free line with a separate no-op line. A later reviewer would likely see it as drift left behind when the committing exemption was removed.

open-question.question: Beyond the three places the goal names, are the CLAUDE.md pipeline listing that tags the skill non-committing, design claim 12's "two exceptions" sentence, and the README's "one runtime prerequisite" sentence with its two host copies under scripts/hosts also updated to record git as a second prerequisite and the bootstrap as committing?
open-question.recommendation: Every statement that the bootstrap does not commit or that Python is the one runtime prerequisite becomes false with this milestone, so the sites are chosen by that grep-checkable rule rather than a hand list: leaving the pipeline tag, design claim 12, or the README and its two host templates unchanged would ship a CLAUDE.md that contradicts itself and a README silent on a requirement the bootstrap now refuses to run without, which defeats the goal of retiring the exemption everywhere.
open-question.alternative: Update every place that states the bootstrap's non-committing exemption or calls Python the single runtime prerequisite. That covers the three sites the goal names and the four the question lists: the CLAUDE.md pipeline tag "non-committing" on line 51, design claim 12's "two exceptions" sentence (which drops to the one failed-run exception), README.md line 54, and its copies in scripts/hosts/claude/README.md and scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md. It also covers the "the workflow's one runtime prerequisite" wording in docs/workflow.md line 11 and docs/skill-reference.md line 7. The host READMEs are then rebuilt into hosts/ so the drift gate still passes. No document is left contradicting the new behaviour. Design claim 12 would otherwise go on saying the bootstrap "does not commit and leaves its changes staged", and README.md would keep calling Python the only prerequisite while the bootstrap refuses to run outside a git work tree. The sites are chosen by a rule that a grep can check, not by a hand-kept list, so none is missed. That fits the milestone's aim of retiring the exemption everywhere. It touches the most files, including the user-facing README and its two host templates, so the milestone's diff and review surface grow beyond what the goal wrote. The "one runtime prerequisite" sentence has to be reworded into a two-prerequisite form in four or five places, and those rewordings must stay consistent. How the git requirement is phrased there also depends on how strict the work-tree check turns out to be (for example, whether a subdirectory of a larger repository passes).

Beyond the three sites the goal names, fix only the statements that the bootstrap does not commit: the CLAUDE.md pipeline tag and design claim 12's "two exceptions" sentence. The README's "one runtime prerequisite" sentence and its host copies stay as they are. The git check is treated as a guard against running outside a repository, not as a declared runtime prerequisite. It removes every statement that the change makes false, since both the pipeline tag and claim 12 say outright that the bootstrap does not commit. The user-facing README and the two scripts/hosts templates, which feed the published distribution repos, are left alone. The change stays close to the goal's wording. The docs end up disagreeing on what Cairn needs: the README, docs/workflow.md line 11 and docs/skill-reference.md line 7 still say Python is the one prerequisite, while the bootstrap stops with a remedy when git is missing. A user who reads the README's prerequisite section first will not learn about the git requirement until the bootstrap refuses to run. Calling git a "guard" rather than a prerequisite is a line the skill's own stop message may blur.

Update only the three places the goal names: the CLAUDE.md invariant, the exemption paragraph in docs/workflow.md, and the skill reference. The CLAUDE.md pipeline tag, design claim 12 and the README prerequisite sentences are left for a follow-up, or for a later review pass to raise. It keeps to exactly the scope the goal wrote, so the milestone's docs work is small and predictable and nothing outside the stated boundary changes. Stale, now-false statements go out with the release. CLAUDE.md would contradict itself: line 51 would still tag the skill "non-committing" under a corrected invariant on line 95. Design claim 12 would still promise an exemption that no longer exists, and the README would stay silent on the new git requirement. That defeats the goal's aim of recording that every file-changing skill commits, and it leaves a known inconsistency for someone to find later.

open-question.question: Should docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md gain a chain that starts from an empty repository with the bootstrap line, now that the bootstrap commits and a headless chain can include it without leaving files behind, or do the chains keep assuming an already-bootstrapped repository?
open-question.recommendation: A short section before "Starting a milestone" that runs the bootstrap line and a define-milestone-goal line from a fresh repository, naming git init and /init as prose preconditions, is what makes the milestone's point visible on the one page about unattended runs, giving an end-to-end path that a bootstrap-only section would not; the extra placeholder costs one legend line, and the chain's clean-tree claim holds because the bootstrap commits the /init-written CLAUDE.md with its own edit.
open-question.alternative: Add a new section to docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, placed before "Starting a milestone", that runs from a fresh git repository through the bootstrap line and `define-milestone-goal "<goal>"`, and hands off to the existing "Starting a milestone" chain. The prose would name `git init` and `/init` as preconditions instead of putting them in the fenced block. It covers the whole headless lifecycle, from an empty repository to a finished milestone, and it shows the milestone's point: with the exemption gone, every documented chain leaves a clean tree. That makes design claim 12's clean-tree promise visible in the one page about unattended runs. It adds a new placeholder, `<goal>`, to a page whose legend defines only `<milestone_id>` and `<project-root>`, so the notation section grows too. The steps that come before the bootstrap (git init, and /init writing CLAUDE.md) cannot be `/cairn:<skill>` lines under the page's "every line is a complete invocation" rule. And if /init leaves an uncommitted CLAUDE.md, the chain's clean-tree claim holds only if the pre-existing dirty-paths question is settled so the bootstrap handles that file safely.

Add a short section, "Bootstrapping a project", whose fenced block holds just the one `claude -p "/cairn:init-milestone-base-workflow"` line, like the one-line "Finishing a milestone" section. Its sentences say to run it once in a git repository after /init, and that it leaves its scaffold committed. It documents the only skill a headless run could call that no chain covers, without adding a placeholder or breaking the page's line rule. It follows a pattern the page already uses (a one-line section), so the added text stays small and cannot go stale on define-milestone-goal's argument. It is not really a chain, so the page still gives no end-to-end path from an empty repository. A reader who wants to go on to a first milestone has to write the define-milestone-goal step themselves. Documenting a run that happens once per project arguably gains little over the README's existing setup instructions.

Put the bootstrap line at the top of the existing "Starting a milestone" chain. The skill is idempotent and stops without changes on an already-bootstrapped project, so the same chain would work on the first milestone and on every later one. No new section. One chain then works whether or not the repository has been bootstrapped, and the run cannot fail later because the scaffold is missing. It does not help an empty repository by itself: the chain's goto-next-milestone line still needs a milestone already defined, and that has to come after the bootstrap. So the chain's own precondition ("a milestone is defined and the pointer reads none") contradicts the bootstrap line in front of it. It also adds a headless model run, with its prerequisite checks, to every milestone start just to reach a no-op on every run after the first. Whether that no-op run prints a distinct line depends on how the reporting-shape question is settled.

Leave docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md without a bootstrap chain: every chain keeps assuming a bootstrapped repository, and at most one sentence in the page's opening paragraph notes that the bootstrap runs once beforehand. The milestone's scope stays at the three places the goal names. It avoids documenting a step that happens once and is usually interactive (it usually follows /init and a conversational discuss-milestone-goal) on a page meant for repeatable unattended runs. It also leaves nothing on the page that depends on how the sibling questions about subject, reporting, and dirty paths are settled. It passes up the change the goal is about: once the bootstrap commits, it is safe in a headless chain, and the page would still not say so. A reader could reasonably assume from the old exemption that the bootstrap has to stay manual. The page's claim that "every skill commits what it changes" also stays untested for the one skill that only now meets it.

open-question.question: Does the git prerequisite pass whenever the workspace root is inside any git work tree (for example a subdirectory of a larger repository), or only when the workspace root is itself the repository's top level, and does a freshly initialized repository with no commits yet pass?

depends-on.question: Git-check remedy wording
depends-on.option: Four-part stop, user runs git init

open-question.recommendation: One `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` probe asks for exactly what the shared commit procedure needs, which works from a subdirectory and on an unborn HEAD, so monorepo subprojects and brand-new repositories pass and a plain "git init, then re-run" remedy is sufficient; top-level-only refuses correct subprojects and invites a nested git init, commit-required enforces nothing the procedure needs, and a nested-repository advisory lands after the commit has already gone where the enclosing repository's own log shows it.
open-question.alternative: The check passes whenever the workspace root is inside any git work tree. That covers a subdirectory of a larger repository and a freshly initialized repository with no commits yet. A single probe such as `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` decides it, and no commit is required to exist. The check asks for exactly what the shared commit procedure needs and nothing more. That procedure's path-scoped `git status --porcelain -- <PATHS>`, `git add` and `git commit` all work from a subdirectory and on an unborn HEAD, where the bootstrap commit simply becomes the root commit. Monorepo subprojects are served, and a plain "git init, then re-run" remedy is enough to pass. If the workspace root happens to sit inside an enclosing repository the user never meant to use (for example a home directory tracked as a dotfiles repository), the check passes silently. The bootstrap commit, and every later skill's commit, then lands in that outer repository with no warning.

The check passes only when the repository's top level (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`) is the workspace root itself. A freshly initialized repository with no commits still passes. A workspace root that is only a subdirectory of a larger work tree stops before any write, like the Python check. It rules out committing into an accidental enclosing repository. Every Cairn commit then goes to a repository rooted exactly where `milestones/` and `CLAUDE.md` live, which matches the workflow's assumption that everything is anchored at the workspace root. It refuses monorepo subprojects that the commit procedure would handle correctly. The obvious remedy for such a project, running `git init` in the subdirectory, creates a nested repository, which is worse than the case it guards against. Comparing the two paths also has to cope with symlinked or aliased paths (such as `/var` versus `/private/var` on macOS), or it can fail a root that is really correct.

The check passes inside any git work tree, including a subdirectory, but only once HEAD resolves to at least one commit. A freshly initialized repository with no commits stops, with a remedy asking for an initial commit first. The bootstrap commit never becomes the project's root commit, so the repository's history starts with the user's own content rather than with Cairn scaffolding. The commit procedure never needs this, so the check is stricter than any requirement it enforces. It also makes "git init, then re-run" insufficient on its own: whether that is acceptable depends on how the remedy wording is settled. Either way, the user gets an extra manual step before a brand-new project can be bootstrapped.

alternative.id: Any work tree, advise when nested

open-question.alternative: The check passes inside any git work tree, including one with no commits yet. When the repository's top level differs from the workspace root, the bootstrap still proceeds but also prints an advisory naming the enclosing top level. Monorepo subprojects and fresh repositories are served as in the permissive option. The one case that risks committing into an unintended enclosing repository is still made visible to the user, without refusing it. The advisory does not block, so the scaffolding commit has already landed in the enclosing repository by the time the user reads it. It also adds an output line beyond the single fixed status line the committing skills print. Whether that extra line is allowed depends on how the bootstrap's reporting shape is settled.
